Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: You get a frantic call from your friend whose car has broken down on the side of the highway late at night, and they need you to come get them immediately.
Situation2: They organize an intensive workshop for community leaders to deeply understand and apply complex theological concepts.
Story: It was nearly midnight when my phone buzzed, jolting me from the last bits of preparation for tomorrow’s workshop. I glanced at the screen—Ben. His voice trembled as he explained his car had broken down on the highway, miles from town, and he needed me to come get him. As his friend, I knew he had no one else to call, and I could hear the panic in his voice. But tomorrow, I was leading the most important workshop of my pastoral career, one that required me to be sharp, rested, and ready to guide community leaders through challenging theological concepts. The church had entrusted me with this responsibility, expecting me to embody the principles I teach—commitment, diligence, and leadership. Yet, as Ben’s friend, I was expected to drop everything and help him in his moment of need. My mind raced, torn between the urgent call of friendship and the weighty expectations of my pastoral role. I stared at the phone, heart pounding, feeling the pressure of two worlds pulling me in opposite directions.
